blocks.html: Suppose a teacher wants to store the marks of 40 students. Declaring 40 separate variables — m1 , m2 , … m40 — is tiring, and a loop cannot go through them. An array solves this.
An array is a collection of elements of the same data type, stored in continuous memory locations under one name. Each element is reached by its position number, called the index or subscript.

blocks.code: data_type array_name[size];

rows: Five integers: marks[0] to marks[4] (values not yet set)

blocks.caption: Figure 16.1 · A one-dimensional array in memory

items.html: The first index is 0 and the last index is size − 1.
The size must be a constant known when the program is compiled.
Memory used = number of elements × size of one element. With 4-byte int , int a[10] uses 40 bytes.
C++ does not check whether an index is inside the array. Writing marks[5] in a 5- element array is a serious mistake that may corrupt other data.

lessons.title: 16.2 Reading and processing an array with loops

blocks.html: A for loop with the index running from 0 to size − 1 visits every element. This is called traversing the array.

blocks.text: Program 16.1: Marks of 5 subjects — total and average

blocks.code:
Marks in Hindi: 78
Marks in English: 85
Marks in Maths: 90
Marks in Science: 88
Marks in Computer: 92

Total   = 433 / 500
Average = 86.6

blocks.html: The two arrays subject and marks are parallel arrays: the same index refers to the same subject in both.

lessons.title: 16.3 Finding the largest and smallest element

blocks.html: Assume the first element is both the largest and the smallest, then compare it with every other element. Storing the position (index) rather than the value lets us also print which element it was.

blocks.text: Program 16.2: Hottest and coolest day of a week

blocks.code:
Hottest day : Fri (42.3 C)
Coolest day : Sun (36.9 C)

blocks.html: Linear search checks the elements one by one from the beginning until the required value (the key) is found or the array ends. It works on any array, sorted or not. For n elements it needs at most n comparisons.

blocks.text: Program 16.3: Searching for a roll number

blocks.code:
Enter roll number to search: 113
Found at index 4 (position 5)

Enter roll number to search: 115
115 is not in the list.

blocks.html: The value −1 is used as a signal meaning “not found”, because no real index can be negative.

Sorting means arranging elements in ascending (smallest first) or descending order. Bubble sort compares each pair of adjacent elements and swaps them if they are in the wrong order. After the first pass the largest element has “bubbled” to the last position; after each further pass one more element reaches its final place. An array of n elements needs at most n − 1 passes.

blocks.text: Program 16.4: Bubble sort, showing every pass

blocks.html: The array was already sorted after pass 3. A smarter version stops early when a whole pass makes no swap — try it in the workshop. To sort in descending order, change > to < in the comparison.

An array is passed to a function by writing its name without brackets. The parameter is written with empty brackets, and the size is passed separately. The function works on the original array, not a copy, so any change it makes is visible to the caller.

blocks.text: Program 16.5: Average runs and matches above average

blocks.code:
Average runs per match : 42.4
Matches above average  : 5

blocks.html: Check: the total is 424, so the average is 424 ÷ 10 = 42.4; the scores above it are 45, 78, 101, 56 and 67.

A two-dimensional (2D) array stores data as a table of rows and columns, like a marks register or a spreadsheet. int marks[3][4]; has 3 rows and 4 columns, that is 3 × 4 = 12 elements. The element in row i and column j is written marks[i][j] . Nested loops are used: the outer loop for rows, the inner loop for columns.

blocks.text: Program 16.6: Marks of 3 students in 4 subjects

blocks.code:
Name      Sub1  Sub2  Sub3  Sub4   Total
Riya        78    85    90    88     341
Aman        66    72    81    58     277
Sana        88    91    79    94     352
Average   77.3  82.7  83.3  80.0

blocks.html: Row totals are found by adding across a row; subject averages by adding down a column.
setw() from <iomanip> sets the width of each column so the table lines up.
A string is a sequence of characters such as a name, an address or a sentence. C++ offers two ways to store text:

rows: A char array ending with the null character'\0'
An object of the string class from<string>

blocks.html: In this book we use the string class, which is safer and easier.
cin >> s stops reading at the first space, so it reads only one word. Use getline(cin,
s) to read a full name or sentence.

blocks.text: Program 16.7: Working with the string class

blocks.code:
Place          : Patna, Bihar
Length         : 12
First letter   : P
substr(0, 5)   : Patna
find("Bihar")  : 7
Bihar comes before Patna in dictionary order
After replace  : Gaya, Bihar

blocks.html: The length 12 counts the comma and the space too. Strings are compared character by character using their codes, so "Bihar" < "Patna" because 'B' comes before 'P'.

lessons.title: 16.9 Processing a string character by character

blocks.html: A string behaves like an array of characters, so a loop can examine each character. The functions of <cctype> from Chapter 15 — isalpha() , isdigit() , tolower() ,
toupper() — are very useful here.

Vowels     : 6

blocks.text: Program 16.9: Reverse a word and check for a palindrome

blocks.html: A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards, such as "madam", "level" or "malayalam".

blocks.code:
Enter a word: madam
Reverse: madam
madam is a palindrome.

Enter a word: computer
Reverse: retupmoc
computer is not a palindrome.

lessons.title: 16.10 Using an array as a set of counters

blocks.html: An array can hold one counter for each category. The value read from the user decides which counter to increase. This idea is used in vote counting, survey analysis and frequency tables.

blocks.text: Program 16.10: Counting votes in a school election

blocks.code:
Candidates: 1-Riya 2-Aman 3-Sana 4-Vikas
Enter votes one by one (0 to stop):
1 3 2 1 3 3 5 4 1 3 2 0
Riya : 3
Aman : 2
Sana : 4
Vikas : 1
Invalid votes: 1
Winner: Sana

blocks.html: The vote 5 is outside 1–4, so it is counted as invalid. A value used only to mark the end of input, like 0 here, is called a sentinel value.

Did you know? The Election Commission of India's EVMs work on the same idea: each candidate button increases its own counter, and the counters are read out on counting day. One Ballot Unit has 16 candidate buttons, so in effect it keeps an array of 16 counters.

blocks.html: Aim: To solve everyday problems with arrays and strings.

Alphabetical order. Sort an array of 6 student names using bubble sort. (Strings can be compared with > .)
Matrix addition. Read two 3 × 3 matrices and print their sum using nested loops.
Word counter. Read a sentence with getline() and count its words, assuming words are separated by single spaces.
An array is a collection of same-type elements stored in continuous memory under one name; indices run from 0 to size − 1.
Loops traverse arrays to read, print, total, average and find the maximum and minimum.
Linear search checks elements one by one; bubble sort repeatedly swaps adjacent elements that are out of order.
Arrays are passed to functions by name; the function works on the original array, and the size is passed separately.
A 2D array stores a table; a[i][j] is the element in row i, column j, processed with nested loops.
The string class supports + , == , < , length() , substr() , find() and
